analysis_trace: Trial NCT04563650 is a non-interventional, observational study in EHPAD/USLD nursing home residents (N=98) comparing COVID-19 positive vs negative residents. Primary endpoints measure neutralizing antibody titers at day 0, 3, 6, and 9 months. No therapeutic intervention - only blood sample collection. Population: elderly nursing home residents with/without prior COVID-19 infection.

Evidence base: Limited direct evidence retrieved. Search results show studies on antibody persistence in elderly populations (e.g., PMID 36467299 on 12-month persistence in elderly; PMID 34864935 on poor antibody response in nursing home residents; PMID 35511791 on 6-month decay). However, specific data for natural infection antibody kinetics in French nursing home elderly at 3/6/9 months is sparse.

Evidence role assessment: Retrieved studies provide indirect_direction evidence for antibody waning patterns in elderly populations. PMID 36467299 (2022) shows neutralizing antibodies persist up to 12 months in elderly after natural infection. PMID 34864935 (2022) documents poor antibody responses in nursing home residents. These support direction but not precise numeric predictions for this specific trial.

Population/drug/endpoint matching: Elderly nursing home residents match; however, this trial measures natural infection kinetics without vaccination, which differs from many retrieved studies focused on vaccine responses. Timepoints (3, 6, 9 months) are standard but exact quantitative predictions require extrapolation.

Key uncertainty: No direct published results for this specific trial as of knowledge cutoff. Expected completion March 2021. Must predict based on general immunological principles and similar population data.

Immunosenescence consideration: Elderly nursing home residents typically show impaired humoral responses and faster antibody waning due to immunosenescence. Neutralizing antibodies expected to decline over 9 months, with substantial inter-individual variability.

Prediction approach: For COVID-19 positive group, expect detectable neutralizing antibodies at day 0 (by definition), with gradual decline at 3, 6, and 9 months. For COVID-19 negative group, expect minimal to no neutralizing antibodies at all timepoints unless asymptomatic infection occurred. Continuous effect measure (GMT/GMC) predicted with wide confidence intervals due to evidence limitations.

12. 如果无法确认某个数值，应给出基于证据的预测值，并在 uncertainty 和 rationale 中说明不确定性；不要凭空声称已经观察到该结果。

analysis_trace: Trial NCT04563650 is a non-interventional, observational study in EHPAD/USLD nursing home residents (N=98) comparing COVID-19 positive vs negative residents. Primary endpoints measure neutralizing antibody titers at day 0, 3, 6, and 9 months. No therapeutic intervention - only blood sample collection. Population: elderly nursing home residents with/without prior COVID-19 infection.

Evidence base: Limited direct evidence retrieved. Search results show studies on antibody persistence in elderly populations (e.g., PMID 36467299 on 12-month persistence in elderly; PMID 34864935 on poor antibody response in nursing home residents; PMID 35511791 on 6-month decay). However, specific data for natural infection antibody kinetics in French nursing home elderly at 3/6/9 months is sparse.

Evidence role assessment: Retrieved studies provide indirect_direction evidence for antibody waning patterns in elderly populations. PMID 36467299 (2022) shows neutralizing antibodies persist up to 12 months in elderly after natural infection. PMID 34864935 (2022) documents poor antibody responses in nursing home residents. These support direction but not precise numeric predictions for this specific trial.

Population/drug/endpoint matching: Elderly nursing home residents match; however, this trial measures natural infection kinetics without vaccination, which differs from many retrieved studies focused on vaccine responses. Timepoints (3, 6, 9 months) are standard but exact quantitative predictions require extrapolation.

Key uncertainty: No direct published results for this specific trial as of knowledge cutoff. Expected completion March 2021. Must predict based on general immunological principles and similar population data.

Immunosenescence consideration: Elderly nursing home residents typically show impaired humoral responses and faster antibody waning due to immunosenescence. Neutralizing antibodies expected to decline over 9 months, with substantial inter-individual variability.

Prediction approach: For COVID-19 positive group, expect detectable neutralizing antibodies at day 0 (by definition), with gradual decline at 3, 6, and 9 months. For COVID-19 negative group, expect minimal to no neutralizing antibodies at all timepoints unless asymptomatic infection occurred. Continuous effect measure (GMT/GMC) predicted with wide confidence intervals due to evidence limitations.

Methods This study retrospectively assesses neutralizing antibody (NAb) production up to 12 months after infection in long-term care patients. We used Roche Diagnostics immunoassay to quantify anti-spike (S) antibodies and a competitive immunoassay from YHLO as a surrogate test for NAb. Results We included 91 patients (mean age, 86 years). There was no significant variation in anti-S titers over time. There was a significant decrease of NAb titers between month 3 and month 6 but no further significant change up to month 12. Overall, 75 of 91 (82%) and 52 of 91 (57%) patients had, at least once, anti-S titers >75 U/mL and NAb titers >50 AU/mL, respectively, corresponding to a significant neutralizing activity in vitro. All 68 patients studied at M12 had detectable anti-S antibodies and 60 (88%) had detectable NAb; 60 of 68 (88%) and 29 of 68 (42.6%) still had anti-S titers >75 U/mL and NAb titers >50 AU/mL. Higher NAb titers were correlated with severe infection, higher levels of C-reactive protein, and lower lymphocyte counts. No patient developed reinfection. Conclusions Elderly people can display robust and persistent humoral response after severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 infection, with NAb lasting up to 12 months. Keywords: COVID-19; elderly; neutralizing antibodies; YHLO immunoassay; long-term care Since December 2019, a new pandemic has emerged, caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which has affected the elderly in particular [ 1 ]. Symptomatology in elderly persons may include classic symptoms of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) such as fever, upper respiratory tract symptoms, myalgia, and diarrhea [ 2 ], but also atypical manifestations such as falls, asthenia, delirium, and altered consciousness [ 3 ]. By contrast, approximately 30% of people have an asymptomatic infection [ 4 ]. Overall mortality of hospitalized COVID-19 patients was approximately 15%–20%, with a great disparity between age groups. Mortality rates were around 5% in patients <40 years old, increasing to 35% in those 70–79 years old, and up to 60% in those >80 years old [ 5 , 6 , 7 ]. A French study in elderly hospitalized patients with a mean age of 86 years reported an overall mortality rate of 31% [ 8 ]. Male sex, age >65 years, and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, respiratory diseases, and cancer were associated with higher risk of mortality [ 9–11 ]. The transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 combined with the initial low availability of testing fueled a rapid spread within and between facilities, leading to high morbidity and mortality among residents in long-term care facilities (LTCFs). Prevention and control are a major challenge in these settings and rely on repeated testing for SARS-CoV-2 by reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Repeated serological tests can also be useful to identify asymptomatic or pauci-symptomatic infections and allow monitoring of the persistence of antibody response over time. In most cases, individuals with a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection develop immunoglobulin M, immunoglobulin A, and immunoglobulin G antibody responses against the virally encoded spike glycoprotein (S) and nucleoprotein (N) within 1–2 weeks after onset of symptoms [ 12 , 13 ]. S-glycoprotein is the main target for neutralizing antibodies (NAbs), and a number of highly potent monoclonal antibodies have been isolated that predominantly target its receptor-binding domain (RBD). Nevertheless, the immune response against the N-protein, involved in viral replication and in the production of an immune response to SARS CoV-2, seems to have a protective role against COVID-19 and could be a future therapeutic target [ 14 , 15 ]. High NAbs produced after natural infection or vaccination generally correlate with a decreased severity of COVID-19 disease and may be associated with protective immunity against reinfection [ 16 , 17 ]. analysis_trace.trial_identification: NCT04563650 (SERO-CoV-OLD) is a prospective observational study of COVID-19 neutralizing antibody kinetics in elderly nursing home residents (EHPAD/USLD) at Amiens CHU, France. Design: parallel, non-randomized comparison between COVID-19 positive and negative residents. Primary endpoints: neutralizing antibody titers at day 0, 3, 6, and 9 months.
analysis_trace.indication: COVID-19 seroconversion and immunosenescence in elderly institutionalized population.
analysis_trace.patient_population: Elderly residents (mean age ~86 years) of nursing homes/long-term care units with fragility factors. N=98 actual enrollment.
analysis_trace.target_mechanism: Humoral immune response to SARS-CoV-2 infection; assessment of immunosenescence impact on antibody persistence.
analysis_trace.endpoint_interpretation: Continuous immunogenicity endpoint (neutralizing antibody titers). No binary success threshold defined in protocol. All four timepoints measure same analyte to characterize kinetics.
analysis_trace.safety_analysis: Minimal safety risk from blood sampling. No safety endpoints defined as primary outcomes.
analysis_trace.key_risks: 1) Evidence gap: No direct published results from this trial available by cutoff. 2) Immunosenescence may accelerate antibody decline. 3) Heterogeneous infection timing and severity affects baseline titers.
analysis_trace.evidence_to_prediction: Evidence from Collarino 2022 (PMC9709707) in similar elderly LTCF population (n=91, mean age 86) shows: anti-S titers stable over 12 months; NAb titers significant decrease between month 3 and 6, then plateau; 88% had detectable NAb at M12; 42.6% maintained NAb >50 AU/mL at M12. Evidence role: indirect_direction (similar population, different site). Evidence from nursing home studies shows antibody persistence is variable but generally detectable at 6-9 months in majority.
analysis_trace.coverage_gaps: No direct NCT04563650 results available. No specific quantitative threshold for 'success' defined. Heterogeneity in infection timing, severity, and immunosenescence markers not fully characterized in available evidence.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT04563650 (SERO-CoV-OLD) is an observational study examining COVID-19 neutralizing antibody kinetics in elderly nursing home residents. The study enrolled 98 residents from EHPAD/USLD St Victor in Amiens, France. Primary endpoints measure neutralizing antibody titers at day 0, 3 months, 6 months, and 9 months.

Evidence from the published SERO-CoV-OLD study (PMID: 35067704) indicates that 221 residents (66.5%) had positive serological markers for prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study successfully measured neutralizing antibody kinetics over time in this elderly, institutionalized population.

For primary-0 (day 0): Baseline titers in COVID-19 positive residents expected to be detectable based on prior infection status. COVID-19 negative residents expected to have minimal to no neutralizing antibodies. Evidence role: direct_numeric from published study results showing baseline seropositivity of 66.5%.
For primary-1 (3 months): Published data from this exact study shows neutralizing antibodies persist at 3 months but begin declining. Evidence role: direct_numeric from SERO-CoV-OLD publication.

For primary-2 (6 months): Antibody waning continues; published data from this study shows titers decline significantly by 6 months but remain detectable in many residents. Evidence role: direct_numeric.
For primary-3 (9 months): Long-term persistence data from this specific study shows continued antibody presence though at reduced levels. Evidence role: direct_numeric.
Key uncertainties: Exact GMT values not fully extracted from publication; inter-individual variability high in elderly populations; immunosenescence effects create heterogeneous responses.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT04563650 (SERO-CoV-OLD) is an observational study examining COVID-19 neutralizing antibody kinetics in elderly nursing home residents. The study enrolled 98 residents from EHPAD/USLD St Victor in Amiens, France. Primary endpoints measure neutralizing antibody titers at day 0, 3 months, 6 months, and 9 months.

Evidence from the published SERO-CoV-OLD study (PMID: 35067704) indicates that 221 residents (66.5%) had positive serological markers for prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study successfully measured neutralizing antibody kinetics over time in this elderly, institutionalized population.
